processes.description: A round starts when someone in contracts or logistics finds contracts that need to end, or when a counterparty wants out. The requester asks a contract administrator to prepare and send a termination letter, sometimes with a next-day deadline, and other contracts awaiting termination get added to the same request. Counterparties terminating on their side are told to send a letter of termination by fax.
steps: Identify the contract or contracts that need to be terminated.
Check the contract terms for whether and how it can be terminated and what notice applies.
Ask contract administration to prepare and send the termination letter by a stated date.
Prepare the letter and send it to the counterparty, or receive the counterparty's faxed letter.
Update the contract record to show the termination.

automation.approach: A standard termination letter with fields for contract number, counterparty, effective date and notice clause, plus a short intake checklist that confirms the termination terms before the letter goes out and records the date it was sent or received.
automation.rationale: The quotes show repeated requests to prepare and send the same kind of letter, often several contracts at once and against a short deadline. A ready letter with the variable fields marked removes most of the drafting, while the terms check stays with the contract administrator.

work_estimate.rationale: Pulling up each contract and checking its termination and notice terms takes around 10 to 20 minutes, preparing and sending the letter another 10 to 15, and updating the contract record a few more. Several contracts in one request push a round toward the high end. The letter drafting is the part a template takes over; the terms check stays manual.

processes.description: Schedulers and volume staff path deal volumes to contracts and meters in the scheduling systems and link buybacks to the market deals they offset. Rounds start when a buyback is announced, when a monthly path list is sent out for checking, when a storage customer needs a specific withdrawal path, or when one scheduler changes a path another created. Questions about pricing, documentation from the counterparty and whether a buyback exists at all go back and forth until the supply and market deals are attached as a buy/sell and the month's activity is reviewed.
steps: Receive notice of a sale, buyback or pathing requirement from the desk or a customer.
Confirm the deal terms, pricing type and counterparty documentation.
Create or change the path in the scheduling system for the meter and volume.
Attach the supply deal to the market deal to establish the buy/sell or buyback link.
Circulate the monthly path list for others to check for anything out of line.
Review the month's allocations, links and buybacks and correct what is wrong.

stalls.summary: A request about a buyback with no counterparty documentation sat until the requester asked for its status.
Two schedulers working the same industrial pathing disagree on how it should be done, and one expects the other will not agree on the approach.
A storage withdrawal pathing request drew a complaint that its requester should have been driving the work, showing unclear ownership.

contradictions.summary: The same buyback is described differently: one message reports volumes sold back over a period, a reply says the buyback will be in place through year end, and another reply says no swing and no buyback were intended.
The storage pathing request comes from one scheduler, while another party says he should have been the driving force behind it, so who owns that pathing is disputed.

automation.approach: A validation report that compares each month's paths against active deals, flags buybacks with no linked market deal, flags path edits made by someone other than the creator, and lists deals with tiered pricing, so the monthly path list arrives pre-checked. A short procedure fixes who links buybacks and who confirms counterparty documentation.
automation.rationale: Most rounds are a check of whether paths and buyback links match the deals. A checklist for the monthly review, covering links, buybacks, pricing type and documentation, gives schedulers one shared standard and reduces the disagreements and ownership questions the mail shows.

work_estimate.rationale: A round involves looking up the deal and its pricing, creating or changing a path for a meter and volume, attaching supply to market deals, and in the monthly cases reviewing a full path list or a month of allocations and links. Single path changes take around 15 minutes; monthly list reviews take an hour or more. Matching paths and links to deals is what a report can take over; judging the exceptions stays manual.

processes.description: Volume management and allocation staff spot gas that flowed at a meter with no deal, no nomination or unexpected volumes, sometimes months after the flow. They write to the trader or scheduler with the meter, the days and the volume, asking whether a deal exists or should be created, which deal to place the volume on, or whether to adjust or write it off. Answers involve checking the deal system and pipeline statements, calling the counterparty, and occasionally legal. Until a deal is found, volumes sit on a strangers gas contract or unaccounted-for balance, and requesters chase repeatedly.
steps: Spot flow at a meter with no matching deal, no nomination, or volumes out of line with the deal.
Look up deals and nominations for the meter and days in the deal and scheduling systems.
Ask the trader or scheduler whether a deal exists, should be created or should be revised.
Confirm the actual volumes with the counterparty or pipeline where they disagree.
Create, extend or path a deal, or decide to adjust or write off the volume.
Reallocate the volume off the strangers gas or unaccounted-for balance and close the exception.

stalls.summary: Requesters wait on replies and chase repeatedly for status on a meter, sometimes after voicemails, and one escalates in capitals asking for anyone to help resolve the matter.
Resolution depends on outside parties: a scheduler waits for a counterparty contact to call back after speaking with legal before proceeding.
Questions get passed between people without a clear owner: an issue is placed in another person's lap, and requests are redirected to whoever handles or allocates the point.
The same deal and volume questions go round and round between groups without being settled.
System problems create or hide exceptions: mirrored meters misbehave, nothing comes through in the scheduling system, and a change to system defaults is proposed.
Old flow is raised long after the gas moved, with volumes booked to a strangers gas contract while an earlier request for a deal went unanswered.

contradictions.summary: Different people are named as the one who handles meter flow questions: one sender says a named colleague handles it, another says a different person allocates the point, another names the volume management contact, and another says to talk to the desk lead.
Logistics claims it will inform the assets group of meter changes, while volume management staff separately take responsibility for adjustments, so the duty to communicate and correct is split.
The deal system and the pipeline disagree on volumes: discrepancies with the pipeline are listed by day, and a counterparty agrees volumes should have gone elsewhere than recorded.

automation.approach: A daily exception report that matches measured meter flow against deals and nominations and lists each meter, day and volume with no deal, with the last deal at that meter and its trader attached. A routing table names the owner for each meter or point, and a standard request message carries the meter, days, volume and proposed action, with ageing so old items surface before they go stale.
automation.rationale: Requests are written by hand in the same shape again and again: meter, dates, volume, last deal, question. A request form or tracker layout with those fields and a named owner per point cuts lookup and rewriting, and the ageing column addresses the chasing and handoff confusion the mail shows. Deciding how to book the flow stays with people.

work_estimate.rationale: Each round involves looking up deals and nominations for the meter and days, checking pipeline statements or calling the counterparty, deciding where the volume goes, then creating or pathing a deal and reallocating off the strangers gas or unaccounted balance. Simple flow-with-no-nom cases take around 20 minutes; disputed or old volumes needing counterparty or legal checks run past an hour. Matching flow to deals and finding the last deal are mechanical; the booking decision is not.
